# Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow {.unnumbered}

{{< include "../includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

The brain is not static inside the skull. With every heartbeat it moves, the
blood surges through the cerebral arteries and drains through the venous sinuses,
and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is pushed and pulled through the ventricles and
subarachnoid spaces. These pulsations are a nuisance for functional imaging — they
add cardiac-frequency noise to the signal — but they are also a measurement
opportunity. This resource collects a few methods that image the beating,
flowing brain, and the anatomy of the fluid compartments they probe.

## Amplified MRI

Cardiac-driven brain motion is small, but it can be made visible. Amplified MRI
(aMRI) takes retrospectively cardiac-gated MRI data and exaggerates the tiny
frame-to-frame displacements, much as Eulerian video magnification amplifies
subtle motion in ordinary video. A phase-based amplification algorithm improves
on the original intensity-based approach, producing a clearer, less noisy
visualization of how the brain deforms over the cardiac cycle.

![Amplified MRI (aMRI): cardiac-driven brain motion, exaggerated for

## The fluid compartments

To interpret these signals it helps to keep the brain's fluid compartments in
mind (@fig-brainbeats-glymphatic). By volume the brain is mostly intracellular
fluid (~65%), with interstitial (extracellular) fluid (~15%), CSF (~10%), and
blood (~10%) making up the rest. The blood is separated from the other
compartments by the blood–brain barrier and the blood–CSF barrier, formed by
tight junctions between endothelial or choroid-plexus epithelial cells. CSF is
produced at the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid
spaces, and — in the glymphatic model — exchanges with interstitial fluid along
perivascular routes gated by astrocytic aquaporin-4 channels.

![The brain's fluid compartments and barriers: ventricles and choroid plexus,
the blood–brain barrier, and the blood–CSF barrier (after Jessen et al., "The
Glymphatic System: A Beginner's Guide").](images/brain-beats/glymphatic-compartments.png){#fig-brainbeats-glymphatic}

## Cardiac pulsations in the MR signal

Functional MRI is sensitive to blood flow, oxygenation, and volume, and these
change on two very different time scales (@fig-brainbeats-bold-cardiac). The
familiar BOLD hemodynamic response unfolds over ~10–20 s. Superimposed on it are
much faster cardiac pulsations, once per heartbeat. The clinical motivation —
conditions such as migraine and raised intracranial pressure — is to build a tool
that characterizes the whole-brain distribution and timing of these pulsations
rapidly at 3 T.

![Functional MRI is influenced by blood flow, oxygenation, and volume. The slow
BOLD response (top) and the fast cardiac pulsations (bottom) occur on very
different time scales.](images/brain-beats/bold-vs-cardiac.png){#fig-brainbeats-bold-cardiac}

Resolving pulsations that recur roughly once per second requires fast sampling
and a way to reference the data to the heartbeat (@fig-brainbeats-cardiac-method).
A pulse oximeter on the thumb records the photoplethysmogram (PPG). The fMRI
signal is sampled quickly (here TR = 250 ms, slice acquisition time 50 ms), each
sample is aligned to the nearest heartbeat peak, and the aligned traces are
averaged across many beats. Splitting the data into even and odd heartbeats and
comparing the two averages gives a direct estimate of the measurement's
reliability.

![Measuring cardiac pulsations. A thumb pulse oximeter (A) provides the heartbeat
reference for the rapidly sampled fMRI signal (B); traces are aligned to heartbeat
peaks (C) and averaged, with even/odd splits used to assess reliability
(D).](images/brain-beats/cardiac-method.png){#fig-brainbeats-cardiac-method}

## Where the flow happens

The pulsations are ultimately driven by the cerebral circulation. Arterial blood
arrives through the carotid and basilar arteries and is distributed by the
anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries; venous blood drains through
the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses (@fig-brainbeats-blood-flow).
Directly imaging the vascular pulsation over a single heartbeat shows the
negative MR signal changes propagating through the vasculature
(@vid-brainbeats-vasculature).

![Blood flow schematic: arterial supply (carotid/basilar, anterior/middle/
posterior cerebral arteries) and venous drainage (superior sagittal, transverse
sinuses).](images/brain-beats/blood-flow-schematic.png){#fig-brainbeats-blood-flow}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![Vasculature: negative MR pulsations over a single
heartbeat.](images/brain-beats/vasculature-pulsation.mp4){#vid-brainbeats-vasculature width="80%" loop="true" autoplay="true" muted="true"}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![Vasculature: negative MR pulsations over a single heartbeat (video; see the
HTML version for the
animation).](images/brain-beats/vasculature-pulsation.png){#vid-brainbeats-vasculature width="80%"}
:::

The same cardiac cycle drives CSF motion. CSF flows from the lateral ventricles
through the third and fourth ventricles and out into the subarachnoid spaces
(@fig-brainbeats-csf-flow), and this pulsatile flow is increasingly thought to
matter for clearance of metabolic waste from the brain.

![CSF flow schematic: from the lateral and third ventricles through the fourth
ventricle into the subarachnoid spaces.](images/brain-beats/csf-flow-schematic.png){#fig-brainbeats-csf-flow}
